note: Paraphrased summaries for prototyping, NOT legal text. Verify every item against the official source before relying on it. Items marked high_impact must be interpreted by a compliance or legal officer.

items.title: Customer identification and verification
items.text: Regulated entities must identify every customer before establishing an account-based relationship and verify identity using an Officially Valid Document (passport, driving licence, voter ID, proof of Aadhaar possession, NREGA card) or its equivalent e-document, together with PAN or Form 60. Customers must not be allowed to open anonymous or fictitious-name accounts.

items.title: Customer due diligence procedure
items.text: Customer due diligence means obtaining and verifying the customer's identity and address, understanding the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship, and identifying beneficial owners where the customer is not an individual. Due diligence applies at onboarding and continues for the life of the relationship.

items.title: Risk-based customer categorisation
items.text: Each customer must be categorised as low, medium or high risk using documented parameters such as customer type, geography, product, delivery channel and transaction pattern. The intensity of due diligence and monitoring must match the assigned risk category, and the categorisation must be reviewable.

items.title: Enhanced due diligence and PEPs
items.text: High-risk customers, politically exposed persons and non-face-to-face customers require enhanced due diligence: additional identity evidence, source of funds or wealth where relevant, senior management approval before establishing or continuing a relationship with a PEP, and closer ongoing monitoring.

items.title: Beneficial ownership of legal entities
items.text: For companies, partnerships, trusts and other legal entities, the natural persons who ultimately own or control the entity must be identified and verified. A controlling ownership interest is defined by a percentage threshold set in the direction (verify the current figure); where no owner meets the threshold the person exercising control, or the senior managing official, is identified.

items.title: Video-based customer identification (V-CIP)
items.text: V-CIP is a consent-based, live, real-time audio-visual interaction with a trained official. It requires liveness checks, capture of geo-location and timestamp, comparison of the live face with the identity document, a secure end-to-end encrypted channel, recording and retention of the session, and an auditable trail. Pre-recorded video is not acceptable.

items.title: Aadhaar e-KYC and OTP-based onboarding
items.text: Aadhaar-based e-KYC authentication requires the customer's explicit, informed consent. OTP-based e-KYC for non-face-to-face onboarding is permitted only within prescribed balance and transaction limits and the account must be converted to full KYC within the prescribed period.

items.title: Periodic updation (re-KYC)
items.text: KYC information must be periodically updated: at least every two years for high-risk customers, every eight years for medium-risk and every ten years for low-risk customers. Customers must be able to submit self-declarations of unchanged details, and accounts must not be closed without notice for missing updates.

items.title: Central KYC Records Registry
items.text: Regulated entities must upload customer KYC records to the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR) within the prescribed period after onboarding, generate or use the KYC identifier, and fetch existing records from the registry before asking the customer to resubmit documents.

items.title: Record retention
items.text: Identification records and transaction records must be preserved for at least five years after the business relationship ends or the transaction takes place, in a form that can be produced promptly for competent authorities.

items.title: Ongoing transaction monitoring
items.text: Transactions must be monitored on an ongoing basis against the customer's profile and risk category, with alert rules calibrated to risk, documented alert handling, and prescribed threshold reports such as large cash transactions.

items.title: Suspicious transaction reporting to FIU-IND
items.text: Reporting entities must report suspicious transactions to the Financial Intelligence Unit - India promptly after concluding that a transaction is suspicious (the Rules set a short working-day deadline, verify the current figure), must not tip off the customer, and must keep the reasoning for decisions not to report.

items.title: Maintenance of records
items.text: Records of transactions and of client identity obtained during the relationship must be maintained for at least five years from the end of the relationship or the transaction, so that individual transactions can be reconstructed.

items.title: Notice and consent for personal data
items.text: Personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose, with free, specific, informed and unambiguous consent after a clear notice, or under a defined legitimate use such as compliance with a legal obligation. Consent must be as easy to withdraw as to give, and the data fiduciary must be able to show it was obtained.

items.title: Purpose limitation, minimisation and erasure
items.text: Only the personal data necessary for the stated purpose may be collected, and it must be erased once the purpose is served unless a law requires retention. KYC records retained under anti-money-laundering law are a legal-retention case.

items.title: Reasonable security safeguards
items.text: The data fiduciary must protect personal data in its possession or under its control, including data processed by processors, by taking reasonable security safeguards such as encryption, obfuscation or masking, access controls and logging, to prevent a personal data breach.

items.title: Personal data breach notification
items.text: On a personal data breach the data fiduciary must notify the Data Protection Board and each affected data principal in the prescribed form and manner.

items.title: Rights of the data principal
items.text: Data principals have the right to access a summary of their data and processing, to correct and complete it, to request erasure (subject to legal retention), to grievance redress, and to nominate another person to exercise rights.

items.title: Handling of Aadhaar numbers
items.text: Aadhaar numbers may be collected only with the holder's consent for a stated purpose, must not be displayed in full (mask all but the last four digits) and, where stored, must be kept encrypted in a secure vault with reference tokens used elsewhere.

items.title: Risk-based approach (R.1)
items.text: Institutions must identify, assess and understand their money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks and apply measures proportionate to them, with stronger controls for higher risk and permitted simplified measures for lower risk.

items.title: Targeted financial sanctions (R.6)
items.text: Customers and related parties must be screened against applicable sanctions lists, and assets of designated persons must be frozen without delay and reported to the authorities.

items.title: Customer due diligence (R.10)
items.text: Institutions must identify and verify customers using reliable independent sources, identify beneficial owners, understand the purpose and nature of the relationship, and conduct ongoing due diligence including scrutiny of transactions. Accounts in obviously fictitious names are prohibited.

items.title: Record keeping (R.11)
items.text: Transaction records and customer due diligence records must be kept for at least five years and be sufficient to reconstruct transactions and to be made available swiftly to competent authorities.

items.title: Politically exposed persons (R.12)
items.text: Institutions need risk-management systems to determine whether a customer or beneficial owner is a politically exposed person and, for foreign PEPs and higher-risk domestic PEPs, must obtain senior management approval, establish source of wealth and funds, and conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring.

items.title: Reliance on third parties (R.17)
items.text: Institutions may rely on third parties for parts of customer due diligence only if they can obtain the information immediately and are satisfied the third party is regulated and supervised; ultimate responsibility for due diligence stays with the relying institution.

items.title: Reporting of suspicious transactions (R.20)
items.text: If an institution suspects or has reasonable grounds to suspect that funds are the proceeds of crime or linked to terrorist financing, it must promptly report to the financial intelligence unit, and staff are protected from liability and prohibited from tipping off.

items.title: Transparency of beneficial ownership (R.24-25)
items.text: Adequate, accurate and up-to-date information on the beneficial owners of legal persons and arrangements must be obtainable promptly. Institutions should not rely solely on a registry and should verify beneficial ownership against independent sources.

items.title: Customer due diligence and high-risk third countries
items.text: Obliged entities apply customer due diligence when establishing a relationship, may use electronic identification means that meet eIDAS assurance levels, apply enhanced due diligence to business relationships involving high-risk third countries and to PEPs, and keep records for five years after the relationship ends.

items.title: Beneficial ownership register
items.text: Beneficial owners of corporate entities are those holding more than 25 percent of shares or voting rights or otherwise exercising control. Obliged entities must collect proof of registration or an extract of the beneficial-ownership register and report material discrepancies.

items.title: Single EU AML rulebook (applies from 2027)
items.text: Directly applicable AML rules replace much national transposition from July 2027, with harmonised customer due diligence requirements, lower beneficial-ownership thresholds for the highest-risk sectors and stricter limits on anonymous instruments. Plan the design so due diligence rules are configurable, not hard-coded.

items.title: Principles of processing (Art. 5)
items.text: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, collected for specified purposes, limited to what is necessary, kept accurate, stored no longer than necessary, protected with appropriate security, and the controller must be able to demonstrate compliance.

items.title: Lawful basis and special-category data (Art. 6 and 9)
items.text: Processing needs a lawful basis; compliance with an anti-money-laundering legal obligation can be one. Biometric data used to uniquely identify a person is special-category data and needs an additional Article 9 condition such as explicit consent.

items.title: Right to erasure (Art. 17)
items.text: Individuals can ask for erasure of their personal data, but the right does not apply where processing is necessary to comply with a legal obligation such as AML record keeping. Requests must be handled and answered within one month.

items.title: Automated decision-making (Art. 22)
items.text: People have the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, such as automatically rejecting an account application. Where such decisions are permitted, safeguards include the right to human intervention, to express a view and to contest the decision.

items.title: Privacy by design and security of processing (Art. 25 and 32)
items.text: Controllers must build data protection into systems by design and by default and apply appropriate technical and organisational measures, including pseudonymisation and encryption, confidentiality and resilience, and regular testing of effectiveness.

items.title: Breach notification (Art. 33-34)
items.text: A personal data breach must be reported to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware unless unlikely to result in risk, and to affected individuals without undue delay when the risk is high.

items.title: Data protection impact assessment (Art. 35)
items.text: A data protection impact assessment is required before processing likely to result in high risk, including large-scale processing of special-category data such as biometrics and systematic monitoring or profiling of individuals.

items.title: Customer Identification Program
items.text: Before opening an account the institution must collect at minimum name, date of birth, address and an identification number, verify identity within a reasonable time through documentary or non-documentary methods, check government lists, and retain identifying information and verification records for five years.

items.title: Customer due diligence and beneficial ownership
items.text: For legal entity customers, institutions must identify and verify each individual owning 25 percent or more and one individual with significant control, understand the nature and purpose of the relationship to build a risk profile, and conduct ongoing monitoring to identify and report suspicious transactions.

items.title: Suspicious activity reports
items.text: A suspicious activity report must be filed within 30 calendar days of initial detection of facts that may constitute a basis for filing (extendable to 60 days if no suspect is identified). SAR existence is confidential and must not be disclosed to the subject.

items.title: Sanctions screening obligations
items.text: US persons must not deal with property or persons on the Specially Designated Nationals list and must block and report matches. Institutions screen customers at onboarding and on an ongoing basis, including when lists change, with a documented process for resolving potential matches.

items.title: Recordkeeping
items.text: Banks must retain specified records of accounts and transactions, including identification and verification records, for five years in a form that can be retrieved on request.

items.title: Safeguarding customer information
items.text: Financial institutions must maintain a written information-security programme with access controls, encryption of customer information in transit and at rest, multi-factor authentication for access, monitoring and incident response, and must give customers a clear privacy notice.

items.title: Identity proofing assurance levels
items.text: Identity assurance level 2 requires evidence of identity to be validated as genuine and the applicant to be verified as its owner, in person or remotely, using biometric comparison or equivalent, with detection of forged or tampered documents and presentation attacks.

items.title: Biometric presentation attack detection
items.text: Biometric capture used for identity verification should include presentation attack detection (liveness) that is tested against spoofing with photos, replayed video, masks and deepfakes, and report attack-detection error rates.

items.title: Application security verification
items.text: Web and mobile applications should meet verification requirements for authentication, session management, access control, input validation, cryptography, error handling, logging and API security appropriate to the data they protect.

items.title: Information security management controls
items.text: An information security management system should apply controls for access management and least privilege, cryptography, logging and monitoring, secure development, supplier relationships and incident management.

items.title: KYC data retention policy (sample)
items.text: Sample bank policy: KYC identity records and screening results are retained for seven years after relationship end, then securely deleted. Biometric templates are deleted after verification unless a regulator requires retention.

items.title: KYC data access policy (sample)
items.text: Sample bank policy: access to KYC documents and customer identifiers is limited to named roles (onboarding agent, compliance analyst, MLRO) with quarterly access review, and every view of a full identity document is logged.

items.title: Onboarding turnaround and manual review policy (sample)
items.text: Sample bank policy: straight-through onboarding decisions should complete within minutes for low-risk customers, and cases routed to manual review must be assigned and resolved within two business days with the reason recorded.
